membership in [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists ([[def-equinumerous]],

$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable]]).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

$B = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function $B \to A$, the empty function, so
$\lvert A^{\varnothing}\rvert = 1 = \lvert A\rvert^{0}$ **even when
$A = \varnothing$**. If $A = \varnothing$ and $B \ne \varnothing$ there is no
function at all, so $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = 0 = 0^{\lvert B\rvert}$ with
$\lvert B\rvert \ge 1$.

Let $A$ be a finite set ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then:

1. $B$ is finite;
2. $\lvert B\rvert \le \lvert A\rvert$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]);
3. $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ if and only if $B = A$;
4. every injection $f : A \to A$ is a bijection, and every surjection

equinumerous with a proper subset of itself. Clause 4 is its working form, and
**finiteness is exactly the hypothesis that fails in general**: the successor map
is an injection of $\mathbb{N}$ into itself that is not surjective, which is the
false statement recorded on this page's companion.

derivations.claim: Let $B=\{0,1\}$. The shift $j\mapsto j-1$ is a bijection from the conventional index set $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ to the von Neumann natural $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$; for $n=0$ both sets are empty. Thus $[n]$ is finite by [F1]. The set $B$ is bijective with $2$, so it is finite as well. For each $I\in\mathcal S_{n,r}$ define its indicator function $\chi_I:[n]\to B$ by $\chi_I(j)=1$ if $j\in I$ and $0$ otherwise. The map $I\mapsto\chi_I$ is injective because equal indicator functions have equal inverse images of $\{1\}$. Its image is a subset of the finite set $B^{[n]}$, which is finite by [F2] and [F3]. Therefore some natural $k$ is bijective with this image; composing that bijection with $I\mapsto\chi_I$ makes $\mathcal S_{n,r}$ bijective with $k$, so [F1] makes it finite.

If $r=0$, then $\varnothing\in\mathcal S_{n,r}$. If $r>0$, then $\{1,\ldots,r\}\subseteq[n]$ because $r\le n$, and the shift $j\mapsto j-1$ is a bijection from $\{1,\ldots,r\}$ to the von Neumann natural $r$; hence this subset has cardinality $r$ by [F1, F5], so $\{1,\ldots,r\}\in\mathcal S_{n,r}$. Thus $\mathcal S_{n,r}$ is nonempty. By [F5], its cardinality $M:=|\mathcal S_{n,r}|$ is defined; by [F6] and nonemptiness, $M\ge1$. Give each $I\in\mathcal S_{n,r}$ weight $q(I)=1/M$. These weights are nonnegative and their finite sum is $M(1/M)=1$.

The outcome set is finite by step 1.1 and its weights satisfy the conditions in step 1.2, so [F4] makes $(\mathcal S_{n,r},q)$ a finite probability space. The argument includes $n=0$, $r=0$, and $r=n$.

Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable unit space ([[def-measurable-space]]), let $n\ge1$, and fix an observed ordered tuple $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathcal Z$. Its **empirical measure** is the set function
$$P_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{z_i},\qquad P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1\{z_i\in A\}\quad(A\in\mathcal F),$$
where $\delta_{z_i}$ is the Dirac set function from [[def-dirac-measure]]. Repeated observations contribute once for each index at which they occur. The statement that $P_n$ is a probability measure is established in [[lem-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

derivations.claim: For any $A\in\mathcal F$, the finite sum in [F1] is nonnegative by [F2]. Also $P_n(\varnothing)=0$ and $P_n(\mathcal Z)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1=1$.

Let $(A_k)_{k\ge1}$ be pairwise disjoint members of $\mathcal F$. For each fixed $i$, at most one term $\delta_{z_i}(A_k)$ is nonzero, and countable additivity in [F2] gives $\delta_{z_i}(\bigcup_k A_k)=\sum_k\delta_{z_i}(A_k)$. Because the sum over $i$ is finite and there are at most $n$ nonzero terms in the resulting double sum, we may regroup to obtain $P_n(\bigcup_k A_k)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_k\delta_{z_i}(A_k)=\sum_k\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{z_i}(A_k)=\sum_kP_n(A_k)$. Thus $P_n$ is countably additive.
By step 1.1, $P_n$ has total mass $1$, and by step 1.2 it is countably additive and vanishes on the empty set. Therefore it is a measure of total mass $1$, hence a probability measure by [F3].

Let $P_n$ be its empirical probability measure from [[def-empirical-measure]] and [[lem-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]. These are resampling units only when the tuple entries satisfy the unit contract in [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity

derivations.claim: The shift $j\mapsto j-1$ is a bijection from $[n]$ to the von Neumann natural $n$. By [F10]–[F12], $[n]$ is finite with cardinality $n$. Let $\Omega_n=\{f:[n]\to[n]\}$, the set of index vectors. By [F4], $|\Omega_n|=n^n$. Assign weight $n^{-n}$ to each $\omega\in\Omega_n$. The weights are nonnegative and sum to $n^n n^{-n}=1$, so [F2] gives a finite probability space $(\Omega_n,w)$ whose event sigma-algebra contains every subset. Each coordinate map $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and record map $Z_j^*(\omega)=z_{\omega(j)}$ is measurable, because every preimage is a subset of $\Omega_n$; hence each $Z_j^*$ is a random element of $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ by [F6].

For $A_j\in\mathcal F$, put $B_j:=\{i\in[n]:z_i\in A_j\}$. Each $B_j$ is a subset of the finite set $[n]$, so [F13] makes it finite. The event $\{Z_j^*\in A_j\text{ for every }j\}$ consists of the functions $g:[n]\to[n]$ with $g(j)\in B_j$ for every $j$. The shift $\tau:[n]\to n$, $\tau(j)=j-1$, from step 1.1 has inverse $\rho:n\to[n]$, $\rho(k)=k+1$; thus $g\mapsto g\circ\rho$ is a bijection from this event's index functions onto $\prod_{k<n}B_{k+1}$. By [F5] this set has cardinality $\prod_{k<n}|B_{k+1}|$, which is the same product as $\prod_{j=1}^n|B_j|$ under that reindexing. Its probability under the uniform weights is therefore $\prod_{k<n}(|B_{k+1}|/n)=\prod_{j=1}^n(|B_j|/n)$. Taking all events except the $j$th to be $\mathcal Z$ gives $\mathbb P^*(Z_j^*\in A_j)=|B_j|/n=P_n(A_j)$ by [F3] and [F7]. The one-coordinate case of step 2.1 gives each $Z_j^*$ law $P_n$. Since $P_n(\mathcal Z)=1$ and $\mathbb P^*(Z_j^*\in\mathcal Z)=1$, step 2.1 then gives $\mathbb P^*(\bigcap_{j\in J}\{Z_j^*\in A_j\})=\prod_{j\in J}P_n(A_j)$. Examples of sampling units are individuals, matched pairs, clusters, time blocks, and treatment-assignment units.

The declared mechanism also specifies a measurable unit-record space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)$ and represents each unit record as an element of $\mathcal Z$. The record space may be the whole data space or one record-valued component of it; the convention is part of the experiment's sampling or assignment contract.

A **resampling unit** is the complete unit record or predeclared group of records that one draw of a resampling procedure selects. A procedure is **unit-compatible for a stated target** when it declares which records are sampled together and does not split a bundle whose joint sampling or assignment dependence is part of that target's data-generating design. Unit compatibility describes the procedure's input and dependence contract; it does not itself establish exact or asymptotic validity. A validity claim requires a separate theorem with hypotheses matched to the sampling or assignment law, target, and resample-size regime.

The conditional bootstrap law of observed units is a law on resampled data records given the fixed observations. Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage
sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and its law
is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]. Thus
$((\mathcal X,2^{\mathcal X}),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is an
experiment in the sense of [[def-statistical-experiment]]. The assignment
law asserts no response-error model, Gaussian law, superpopulation
randomization, or sampling representativeness beyond the stated finite
assignment mechanism. Its finite full-measure support set is
$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$
since $P_\theta(S_\theta)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)=1$. The record contains the
assigned vector and every unit's response; missing or censored outcomes and
repeated visits require a separately declared observation mechanism. The
inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$
units, not an estimand for a wider population.

Inference in this page holds $\mathcal I$ and $\theta$ fixed and averages
over the declared law $p$; it does not condition on the realized assignment.
The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all
$Y_i(z)$ are fixed, $Z$ is random, $(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ is observed, and
potential responses under unassigned vectors are fixed but latent. The
assignment set, weights, and implemented randomization protocol are
design-controlled and should be checked against protocol records. Assignment
logs and response records are empirically assessable, but those checks do not
prove that the declared law generated the data. Potential outcomes under
unassigned vectors are fixed and latent in the realized record. This does
not imply nonidentifiability from the observed-data law: for each $z$ with
$p(z)>0$, the law assigns mass $p(z)$ to $(z,Y_\theta(z))$, and therefore
determines $Y_\theta(z)$. Assignment invariance on this positive-probability
set is **empirically assessable**, and the theorem tests the stronger
invariance hypothesis on all allowed assignments. Values at assignments
with $p(z)=0$, and restrictions on those values, are **substantively
untestable** from this law, since changing them leaves $P_\theta$ unchanged.
One realized assignment does not reveal responses at other assignments.
These classifications do not make the design or scientific model
empirically true.

In the finite randomized treatment-assignment model
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]], a schedule satisfies
the **Fisher sharp null** when for each unit $i$ there is a value $y_i$ such that
$Y_i(z)=y_i$ for every allowed assignment $z$. The full vector
$y=(y_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}$ is then imputable under every assignment.

A **predeclared ordering score** is a real-valued statistic
$T:\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}\to\mathbb R$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]) fixed before the
assignment and outcomes are inspected. Its upper-tail ordering includes ties:
assignment $z'$ is at least as extreme as $z$ when $T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)$.
For a signed score $S$ and fixed null center $s_0$, the corresponding
two-sided ordering is explicitly $T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$. The center is part
of the predeclared ordering; the sharp null alone does not force $s_0=0$
for an arbitrary signed score. A lower-tail ordering is represented by
using $-S$ as the score. A statistic in this setting is a measurable map in
the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; the full power-set data
sigma-algebra makes every such real-valued map measurable.

In a finite randomized treatment-assignment model, fix any real-valued
predeclared ordering score $T(z,y)$. For observed data $(z,y)$ define
$$p_{\rm rand}(z,y):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)\}.$$
Let $\lambda$ be the uniform probability measure on the Borel subsets of
$[0,1]$. For each $\theta$, equip $\mathcal X\times[0,1]$ with the product
sigma-algebra $2^{\mathcal X}\otimes\mathcal B([0,1])$ and define
$$\widetilde P_\theta(E):=\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)\,\lambda\bigl(\{u\in[0,1]:((z,Y_\theta(z)),u)\in E\}\bigr).$$
Let $U$ be the $[0,1]$ coordinate on this extension. Define
$$p^+(z,y,U):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)>T(z,y)\}+U\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)=T(z,y)\}.$$
For every schedule satisfying the Fisher sharp null and every
$u\in[0,1]$,
$$P_\theta\!\left(p_{\rm rand}(Z,Y_\theta(Z))\le u\right)\le u,$$
whereas the added randomization gives
$$\widetilde P_\theta\!\left(p^+(Z,Y_\theta(Z),U)\le u\right)=u.$$
Thus $p_{\rm rand}$ is a valid finite-sample p-value for the sharp null,

independent uniform randomizer is used. For a two-sided test, take

assignment supplies no Gaussian error law, and this theorem makes no
validity claim under the weak zero-average-effect null from
[[def-finite-population-average-treatment-effect-and-weak-null]] unless it
